description: We are students from Ankara High School of Science. We are interested in space, science and technology. We want to learn new things, share ideas and work together to solve problems.
summary: Our project aims to compare different lunar landing sites by scoring their solar power suitability, direct-to-Earth communication potential, and landing safety on a scale from 0 to 100. It addresses the challenge by allowing users to select a date range, showing when the Sun and Earth are visible from each site, and using these data to calculate suitability scores. This is important because communication, energy, and landing safety are essential for lunar missions. Our tool helps users compare landing sites and plan missions accordingly.
details:
Moonlander is an interactive lunar landing site analysis tool focused on candidate regions near the Moon’s south pole. Users can explore NASA’s Artemis IV candidate regions, select a site from the list, or choose a custom location on the lunar map. They can also select a date range and use the interactive 3D view to explore how the Sun’s and Earth’s positions change over time at the selected site.

The project combines lunar digital elevation model (DEM) data with time-based position and visibility analysis. It uses the JPL Horizons API to obtain the Sun’s and Earth’s elevation angles and azimuths over time. These positions are compared with the local terrain horizon to estimate when each body is visible from a site. Moonlander presents comparison scores for solar power suitability and direct-to-Earth communication potential. It also provides a preliminary terrain-based landing safety assessment using available elevation data. This assessment helps users examine terrain factors such as local slopes, but it is an initial screening and does not guarantee a safe landing.

Moonlander’s creative approach is to make lunar site analysis something users can explore directly. Instead of viewing a static map or separate tables of measurements, users can select a location, move through time, observe the Sun and Earth relative to the 3D terrain, and compare the resulting scores. This connects the underlying data to a visual experience: users can see how a ridge, slope, or date may affect visibility and site suitability.

The project’s intended impact is to help people understand the trade-offs involved in choosing a lunar landing site. Mission planners and researchers can use it to explore candidate locations and dates, while students and the public can use it to better understand how terrain, sunlight, and communication geometry affect lunar missions. Moonlander is intended as a comparison and exploration tool that supports more informed discussion and planning; its preliminary scores do not replace mission-specific engineering analysis.

The project was built with Python for its analysis and web server, and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for its interactive interface and visualizations. NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, and PyProj are used to process numerical, terrain, and location data. The team considered solar access, communication with Earth, local slopes and roughness, DEM coverage and resolution, the limits of preliminary safety assessments, and how to present the results clearly in both Turkish and English.
